title: The way of prayer (CCC 2663–2672)
hookLine: to the Father, through Jesus, in the Spirit

cards: An old paper letter needed three things to arrive. A name on the front: who it's for. A stamp and a carrier: how it travels.
And something inside worth sending. Get one wrong and it sits in a sorting room forever. Catholic prayer has a shape like that, hiding in plain sight.

Listen to how the prayers at Mass end, and the same little pattern keeps turning up: to someone, through someone, in someone. The Catechism lays it out as the way prayer travels. Today: the way of prayer.

teach.b: Start with to. In Catholic teaching, prayer is addressed above all to the Father.
Jesus says so at the Last Supper, in the Douay-Rheims: "if you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you." In my name: that's through.

The Catechism says there's no other way of Christian prayer than Christ; alone or together, aloud or silent, it reaches the Father through Jesus. But Jesus isn't only the road. People pray to him directly, by name.
Paul writes, "That in the name of Jesus every knee should bow."
The Catechism describes a prayer from the Christian East, the Jesus Prayer, which you met on day two hundred forty-two: his name joined to a plea for mercy, repeated slowly.

It calls calling on his name the simplest way of praying always. Then in. Paul admits, "we know not what we should pray for as we ought; but the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings."
When words run out, Catholics say, the Spirit prays inside the one who prays.
So the Church invites people to call on the Spirit every day, with the old words "Come, Holy Spirit," especially at the start and the end of something important. To the Father. Through the Son.
In the Spirit. Catholics hold this as one God, not three, and the prayer moves the way they believe God does.

how: Catholic liturgical prayers are usually addressed to the Father and close through Christ in the Holy Spirit; many Catholics also pray directly to Jesus, some with the Jesus Prayer, and call on the Holy Spirit before important work.

games.q: what does “the way of prayer” mean?
o: prayer sent to each saint in a fixed order
a set path a pilgrim walks while praying
prayer to the Father, through Jesus, in the Spirit

games.q: to, through, in — tap the pairs.
p: his name joined to a plea for mercy

s: the Catechism says Catholics pray only to the Father
prayer goes to the Father through Jesus, but Catholics also pray to Jesus by name and call on the Holy Spirit.
Paul writes that the Spirit prays for us when we don't know what to pray
"the Spirit himself asketh for us with unspeakable groanings."
the Catechism calls calling on the name of Jesus the simplest way of praying always
it describes the Jesus Prayer, repeated slowly, his name joined to a plea for mercy.

games.q: it's the night before he dies, and Jesus is teaching his friends how their asking should go. what does he tell them?
o: ask the Father in my name.
games.why: "if you ask the Father any thing in my name, he will give it you." to the Father, through the Son: the shape the Catechism builds on.

practice: If you pray, turn first to the Father with one short line of your own, then say the name of Jesus slowly, once, then the old words "Come, Holy Spirit," and wait in the quiet after them.
If you don't pray, simply notice three directions: what's above you, what's beside you, and what's within.

wordCard.voice: The way of prayer. In Catholic teaching, prayer goes to the Father, through Jesus and in his name, in the Holy Spirit.

orig.note: Latin: come, Holy Spirit — the old opening words the Church uses to call on the Spirit.

carryVoice: Your line: to, through, in. Three small words, and a whole map of prayer. Back tomorrow, same hill.
